messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame is a 45-year-old agricultural worker who grew up in a household where violence could erupt behind a closed bedroom door at night. He remembers standing in the hallway as a boy, hearing his mother being hit, frozen with the conviction that he should do something and the equally overpowering knowledge that he was small and terrified. What has stayed with him most sharply is not a single image so much as the helplessness of listening, waiting, and doing nothing. In the years since, that moment has hardened into a private verdict: he will never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened. He says he used to be a happy person, but now he feels miserable most of the time, and he has come to believe that whatever faith he once had—in people, in life, even in anything protective beyond himself—has been stripped away.

Those beliefs leave him living as if danger is always close. Because he sees the world as fundamentally unsafe and himself as someone who failed when it mattered, reassurance does not land; even when his partner tells him he is safe, he cannot believe it. He moves through his days superalert, scanning tone of voice, posture, and sudden movement in other people. Night is especially difficult. Darkness brings back the old sense that the worst things happen when others are asleep or out of sight, and he finds it much harder to feel safe after sundown than during the day.

At work in the fields, this vigilance has become woven into ordinary routines. If another worker asks him to check irrigation lines in a more isolated stretch of land or to ride out alone with a supervisor, he finds a way to avoid it. He tries to make sure he is never alone with another person, not because he can easily explain why, but because his body tells him that being by himself with someone means something can turn dangerous without warning. He watches constantly, keeps to open areas when he can, and notices exits, vehicles, and who is nearby. When he gets home in the evening, he checks locks repeatedly and stays more awake than he wants to admit, listening into the night as if alertness itself could prevent harm.

His fear also drives what he does in his own mind. When memories of childhood start to surface, he tries hard not to think about them, cutting them off before they can fully form. Yet the more threatened he feels, the more his thoughts circle back in another direction: long stretches of rumination about how he might get even with the man who hurt his mother. He knows those thoughts do not lead anywhere practical, but when he feels on guard and unsafe, imagining revenge gives him a fleeting sense of not being powerless.

Over time, these habits have deepened the meanings he already gives the trauma. Avoiding being alone with others has narrowed his life and confirmed, in his mind, that people cannot be trusted. His effort to suppress thoughts has not restored any peace; instead, it has left the memory feeling unresolved and his misery more constant. The revenge rumination especially leaves him ashamed afterward, because it pulls him back to the same moral wound—that violence shaped him, and that he still has not found a way to live beyond what he failed to stop. In this way, what he does to manage the fear ends up feeding his sense that he has lost happiness, lost faith, and become a man defined by that childhood inaction.

The cycle has tightened further in recent years. The more watchful he becomes, particularly at night, the more convinced he feels that safety is an illusion and that no one truly understands the danger he senses. That conviction makes him mistrust comfort from his partner and withdraw from closeness, which has strained the relationship. At work, coworkers have noticed that he avoids certain tasks and seems tense whenever he is paired off, and he worries he is being seen as difficult. He finally sought help after his partner told him she could not keep being shut out by his constant guardedness and sleepless nights. Kwame came in afraid that this is simply who he is now—miserable, distrustful, always on guard—but also with a small hope that he might not have to keep living as though that hallway at night is still the place he is trapped.
